comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official study guide establishes a 180-EC bachelor with a common 60-EC first year and two equally weighted specialisations. The generic normalized target does not prefer one route. People, Planet, Power is selected through the neutral official-order tie-break. Its fixed 60-EC second year and 30-EC third-year core are reconstructed, Anthropology of Religion is the first-listed 10-EC exploration choice, and the genuine 30-EC free-elective space is preserved without invented content.
components: Diversity and Development in a Sociological Perspective
Multivariate Analysis: from Data to Report
Personal and Professional Impact for Anthropologists
Genuine elective space preserved without inventing a minor, internship, exchange package or individual electives.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic bachelor and the official guide presents People, Planet, Power and Media Making Movements as equally weighted routes with a common first year. No route is shown as more representative of the whole degree, so the first-listed route is selected independently of UCR fit; its first-listed third-year exploration option, Anthropology of Religion, is used by the same neutral rule.

core: Cultural anthropology and development sociology: cultural meaning, diversity, identity, globalisation and social change
Ethnographic and qualitative research through fieldwork, participant observation, interviewing, ethics, writing and multimodal methods
Anthropological and sociological theory, comparative inquiry, quantitative analysis and an independent bachelor thesis
adjacent: People, Planet, Power: sustainability, development, ecology, politics and power
Media, Making, Movements: media, digital communities, social movements and creative or visual inquiry
Power, inequality, migration, citizenship and global connections
Contemporary public issues, exclusion and community responses to global change
questions: How do people create meaning, identity and social organisation across cultural contexts?
How do power, inequality, migration and development shape everyday experience?
How do ecological change, media technologies and social movements transform communities?

alternatives.label: Anthropology, Culture & Global Change
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum visibly combines culture, society, identity, global change and qualitative inquiry without implying a dedicated ethnographic fieldwork degree.
alternatives.concept: A closest feasible pathway combining cultural difference, identity, development, global change, power, qualitative social research, history, politics, communication and media.
progression: Sociology, history, rhetoric, qualitative research and philosophy foundations precede modern sociology, politics, advanced media, cultural analysis and research seminars. Formal prerequisites and planned offerings pass, with seven 300-level courses.

alternatives.label: Ecology, Communities & Global Change
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum combines social and cultural analysis with climate, sustainability, ecology and community responses to global change.
alternatives.concept: Builds the evidenced People, Planet, Power direction around climate change, sustainability, communities, environmental governance, globalisation, migration and qualitative social research.
progression: Sociology, sustainability, qualitative research and environmental foundations precede political sociology, climate governance, advanced environmental study and research seminars. Formal prerequisites and planned offerings pass, with nine 300-level courses.
alternatives.distinctness: This route makes ecology, climate and community responses the central anthropological application; it differs from both other programmes by more than four courses and 30 EC.

alternatives.label: Media, Visual Culture & Digital Anthropology
alternatives.concept: Builds the evidenced Media, Making, Movements direction around cultural inequality, social movements, visual inquiry, documentary media, digital communities and qualitative research.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines cultural and social theory with film, media, visual inquiry, politics and data analysis; the label states those visible strands directly.
progression: Sociology, history, media and qualitative-research foundations precede politics, advanced visual culture, media analysis and research seminars. Formal prerequisites and planned offerings pass, with six 300-level courses.
alternatives.distinctness: This route centres visual media, digital culture and technology as anthropological objects and methods; it differs from both the broad closest match and the ecology route by more than four courses and 30 EC.

blocks: Both introduce systematic theoretical study of society and social organisation, although Leiden provides a dedicated anthropology-and-sociology sequence.
Both situate cultural and social change historically and transnationally.
Both develop qualitative research design, interviewing, observation, analysis and interpretation; Leiden adds dedicated anthropological field practice.
Both examine modern social theory, diversity, inequality and changing social relations.
Both engage advanced social theory about power, inequality and contemporary societies.
Both require sustained independent research and academic argument, though in different disciplinary settings.
Both use comparison to examine human communities and cultural difference, while archaeology and anthropology retain distinct methods.
UCR qualitative-methods study does not reproduce Leiden's separately credited ethnographic fieldwork component.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Leiden's multivariate-analysis component.
Both analyse states, citizenship, political institutions and power.
Both connect ecological challenges with social and economic systems; Leiden frames this anthropologically.
Both develop clear written argument and communication about cultural and social questions.
Both examine ethical foundations and responsibilities relevant to research on people and societies.
Both develop regionally grounded cultural analysis, though with distinct disciplinary objects and methods.
Both cultivate critical reading and interpretation of academic discourse and meaning.
Both use mediated and visual forms to analyse and communicate social life.
Both introduce quantitative analysis of data, while Leiden's component is oriented to anthropological and sociological research.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Anthropology of Religion.
Both support reflection on academic development, professional identity and future pathways.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Leiden's specialisation-specific research preparation.
Leiden's genuine 30-EC elective space remains open and is not replaced by invented content.

selection.assessment: The closest match owns the programme-defining cultural-anthropology, development-sociology and ethnographic-research interests. People, Planet, Power and Media, Making, Movements are the two formal, evidence-backed specialisation directions and yield feasible, substantively distinct programmes. All generator-eligible interests are owned by the closest match or one of those two candidates, and the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

notes.text: Leiden provides a dedicated anthropology-and-development-sociology curriculum with sequenced anthropological theory, ethnographic methods and fieldwork. UCR can assemble strong cultural and qualitative social-science pathways, but does not reproduce that disciplinary sequence.
Leiden's 30-EC third-year free-elective space is retained without inventing a minor, exchange, internship or individual elective package.
